hero.headline: Treasure Coast voters face local ballot questions Nov. 3 on taxes, services, land
hero.teaser:
Treasure Coast voters will decide five local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from land protection and mosquito control to sales taxes and trash pickup.

In Martin County, two p
hero.body:
Treasure Coast voters will decide five local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from land protection and mosquito control to sales taxes and trash pickup.

 In Martin County, two proposed charter amendments apply only to Stuart voters. One would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard.

 Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve.

 St. Lucie County has three local issues. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years. The current tax is set to expire in 2028.

 Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Port St. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee. The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year.

 The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents' preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change.

 A third St. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy.

 No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River County. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments.

cards.headline: Arsenic hot spot found on Fort Pierce brownfield, not Shelli development site
cards.teaser: New state environmental testing results show the most significant arsenic contamination near Fort Pierce's Fisherman's Wharf sits on a separate city brownfield property, not on the
cards.body:
New state environmental testing results show the most significant arsenic contamination near Fort Pierce's Fisherman's Wharf sits on a separate city brownfield property, not on the waterfront parcel the city sold to developer Chris Shelli, raising questions about the city's earlier claim that contamination could wipe out his damages in an ongoing lawsuit.

 The Florida Department of Environmental Protection found arsenic about 148 times the residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of a former citrus packing house property immediately north of Fisherman's Wharf. St. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site. On the approximately 3.2-acre development parcel the city sold to Shelli, FDEP found arsenic above residential cleanup targets in only two soil samples, both less than twice the target level.

 The city sent Shelli a letter in 2025 arguing the property was likely contaminated and that the cost of remediation essentially eliminates his damages claim. The city made that assertion before FDEP completed its testing. FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels associated with the former citrus packing house property but did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.

 Jordan Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, reviewed the findings and said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming. Beckler said the vast majority of the samples were not that high above the residential standard and noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils.

 Shelli sued Fort Pierce for breach of contract after emails showed city commissioners did not learn until 2023, about two years after the sale, that removing a state right-of-reverter restriction on roughly half the property could cost nearly $2 million. The restriction means the land could revert to the state if sold for private development.

 Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, said questions could remain over what the city knew or should have known and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before purchase.

 Fort Pierce commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli in March. The city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules. Commissioners took no action and the offer was later deemed rejected.

 Mike Jenkins, whose family owns the property beneath 12A Buoy restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf and has owned the property for roughly 50 years, said associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners. A city spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.

cards.headline: Parking dispute sparked Pollo Tropical shooting in Port St. Lucie, police say
cards.teaser: Christopher Harris, 37, who was shot in the chest at a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical on Saturday, now faces battery and aggravated battery charges despite being the shooting victim, according to newly released incident report details.
cards.body:
Christopher Harris, 37, who was shot in the chest at a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical on Saturday, now faces battery and aggravated battery charges despite being the shooting victim, according to newly released incident report details that show the shooting stemmed from a dispute over a parking space.

 Multiple witnesses told police they observed Harris push another man and engage in a verbal argument before the man discharged a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris came back inside the restaurant and asked someone to call 911.

 A witness picking up an Uber order told police she observed a man pull into a parking space before another vehicle pulled into the space in front of them. The witness said that while exiting Pollo Tropical, the man was following someone out, calling them names and lunging toward them. She said she observed something in the man's hand and the man was so close to the other person that they were almost touching before she saw the other person pull out a firearm and shoot.

 A witness picking up a DoorDash order said Harris came into Pollo Tropical yelling at another man over a parking space. The witness said the man exited to get his order, and Harris continued to yell, telling the man to come outside. The witness said Harris held the door open and then approached the man before he heard a gunshot. The witness said the man stated that Harris ran up on him with a knife.

 Officers recovered a 9mm handgun from the scene. The Port St. Lucie Police Department confirmed that Harris, listed as a victim in the report, faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon. Harris will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital.

cards.headline: Fire at Wendy's on Jensen Beach Boulevard caused by burned-out AC fan motor
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue units responded to a fire at a Wendy's restaurant at 1409 NE Jensen Beach Boulevard in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon. The fire was caused by a burne
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue units responded to a fire at a Wendy's restaurant at 1409 NE Jensen Beach Boulevard in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon. The fire was caused by a burned-out fan motor in an air conditioning unit on the roof. The building was safely evacuated, no injuries were reported, and no nearby structures were threatened.

 Units were called to the scene at around 4:30 p.m. on Wednesday after reports of smoke and visible flames coming from inside the restaurant, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The emergency call brought firefighters to the location to investigate the source of the smoke and flames that had been reported by witnesses at the scene.

 Upon arrival, firefighters found white smoke coming from the AC unit on the roof and light to moderate smoke inside the building. Crews worked to locate the source of the fire and discovered it was the air conditioning unit mounted on the roof of the restaurant. After inspecting the unit, firefighters noticed the fan motor had burned out, which was determined to be the cause of the fire and smoke.

 Martin County Fire Rescue successfully extinguished the fire and ensured the building was safe before clearing the scene. The quick response by fire crews prevented the fire from spreading to other parts of the building or threatening nearby structures in the area. No firefighters or civilians were injured during the incident, and the evacuation of the building proceeded without complications.

hero.headline: Fire at Wendy's on Jensen Beach Boulevard caused by burned-out AC fan motor
hero.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue units responded to a fire at a Wendy's restaurant at 1409 NE Jensen Beach Boulevard in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon. The fire was caused by a burne
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue units responded to a fire at a Wendy's restaurant at 1409 NE Jensen Beach Boulevard in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon. The fire was caused by a burned-out fan motor in an air conditioning unit on the roof. The building was safely evacuated, no injuries were reported, and no nearby structures were threatened.

 Units were called to the scene at around 4:30 p.m. on Wednesday after reports of smoke and visible flames coming from inside the restaurant, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The emergency call brought firefighters to the location to investigate the source of the smoke and flames that had been reported by witnesses at the scene.

 Upon arrival, firefighters found white smoke coming from the AC unit on the roof and light to moderate smoke inside the building. Crews worked to locate the source of the fire and discovered it was the air conditioning unit mounted on the roof of the restaurant. After inspecting the unit, firefighters noticed the fan motor had burned out, which was determined to be the cause of the fire and smoke.

 Martin County Fire Rescue successfully extinguished the fire and ensured the building was safe before clearing the scene. The quick response by fire crews prevented the fire from spreading to other parts of the building or threatening nearby structures in the area. No firefighters or civilians were injured during the incident, and the evacuation of the building proceeded without complications.

hero.headline: Arsenic hot spot found on Fort Pierce brownfield, not Shelli development site
hero.teaser: New state environmental testing results show the most significant arsenic contamination near Fort Pierce's Fisherman's Wharf sits on a separate city brownfield property, not on the
hero.body:
New state environmental testing results show the most significant arsenic contamination near Fort Pierce's Fisherman's Wharf sits on a separate city brownfield property, not on the waterfront parcel the city sold to developer Chris Shelli, raising questions about the city's earlier claim that contamination could wipe out his damages in an ongoing lawsuit.

 The Florida Department of Environmental Protection found arsenic about 148 times the residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of a former citrus packing house property immediately north of Fisherman's Wharf. St. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site. On the approximately 3.2-acre development parcel the city sold to Shelli, FDEP found arsenic above residential cleanup targets in only two soil samples, both less than twice the target level.

 The city sent Shelli a letter in 2025 arguing the property was likely contaminated and that the cost of remediation essentially eliminates his damages claim. The city made that assertion before FDEP completed its testing. FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels associated with the former citrus packing house property but did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.

 Jordan Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, reviewed the findings and said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming. Beckler said the vast majority of the samples were not that high above the residential standard and noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils.

 Shelli sued Fort Pierce for breach of contract after emails showed city commissioners did not learn until 2023, about two years after the sale, that removing a state right-of-reverter restriction on roughly half the property could cost nearly $2 million. The restriction means the land could revert to the state if sold for private development.

 Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, said questions could remain over what the city knew or should have known and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before purchase.

 Fort Pierce commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli in March. The city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules. Commissioners took no action and the offer was later deemed rejected.

 Mike Jenkins, whose family owns the property beneath 12A Buoy restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf and has owned the property for roughly 50 years, said associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners. A city spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.

cards.headline: Parking dispute sparked Pollo Tropical shooting in Port St. Lucie, police say
cards.teaser: Christopher Harris, 37, who was shot in the chest at a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical on Saturday, now faces battery and aggravated battery charges despite being the shooting victim, according to newly released incident report details.
cards.body:
Christopher Harris, 37, who was shot in the chest at a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical on Saturday, now faces battery and aggravated battery charges despite being the shooting victim, according to newly released incident report details that show the shooting stemmed from a dispute over a parking space.

 Multiple witnesses told police they observed Harris push another man and engage in a verbal argument before the man discharged a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris came back inside the restaurant and asked someone to call 911.

 A witness picking up an Uber order told police she observed a man pull into a parking space before another vehicle pulled into the space in front of them. The witness said that while exiting Pollo Tropical, the man was following someone out, calling them names and lunging toward them. She said she observed something in the man's hand and the man was so close to the other person that they were almost touching before she saw the other person pull out a firearm and shoot.

 A witness picking up a DoorDash order said Harris came into Pollo Tropical yelling at another man over a parking space. The witness said the man exited to get his order, and Harris continued to yell, telling the man to come outside. The witness said Harris held the door open and then approached the man before he heard a gunshot. The witness said the man stated that Harris ran up on him with a knife.

 Officers recovered a 9mm handgun from the scene. The Port St. Lucie Police Department confirmed that Harris, listed as a victim in the report, faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon. Harris will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital.
